claim: Previous studies of laboratory strains of budding yeast showed that when gene copy number is altered experimentally, RNA levels generally scale accordingly.
source: Previous studies of laboratory strains of budding yeast had shown that when gene copy number is altered experimentally, RNA levels generally scale accordingly.
evidence: This is a statement about previous research findings, supported by the context of the manuscript and citations throughout the paper.

claim: The tight correlation between gene copy number and RNA levels is true when the copy number of individual genes or entire chromosomes is altered.
source: This is true when the copy number of individual genes or entire chromosomes is altered.
evidence: This extends the previous claim about the correlation between gene copy number and RNA levels to different types of genetic alterations.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) reported that the tight correlation between gene copy number and RNA levels is not observed in recently isolated wild Saccharomyces cerevisiae variants.
source: In a recent study, Hose et al. (2015) reported that this tight correlation between gene copy number and RNA levels is not observed in recently isolated wild Saccharomyces cerevisiae variants.
evidence: This is a direct statement about findings from a cited study.

claim: Reexamination of the Hose et al. data revealed a tight correlation between gene copy number and gene expression in wild S. cerevisiae strains.
source: In contrast to the results of Hose et al., our reexamination of their data revealed a tight correlation between gene copy number and gene expression.
evidence: This is the main finding of the current study, supported by the data analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Widespread dosage compensation occurs neither in laboratory strains nor in natural variants of S. cerevisiae.
source: We conclude that widespread dosage compensation occurs neither in laboratory strains nor in natural variants of S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the reanalysis of data presented in the results section.

claim: Changes in gene copy number result in changes in gene expression in budding yeast, fission yeast, mammalian cells, and plants.
source: Gene expression studies in budding yeast, fission yeast, mammalian cells, and plants revealed that this is due to the fact that changes in gene copy number result in changes in gene expression (Chikashige et al., 2007; Huettel et al., 2008; Pavelka et al., 2010; Sheltzer et al., 2012; Stingele et al., 2012; Torres et al., 2010; 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: In haploid budding yeast strains harboring single chromosome gains, RNA levels of more than 90% of genes located on the extra chromosome reflect the increased gene copy number.
source: For example, in haploid budding yeast strains harboring single chromosome gains, RNA levels of more than 90% of genes located on the extra chromosome reflect the increased gene copy number (Dephoure et al., 2014; Torres et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding from cited previous studies.

claim: Histone and some ribosomal genes do not show RNA levels that reflect increased gene copy number in aneuploid yeast.
source: Only few genes, such as histone and some ribosomal genes defy this trend (Dabeva and Warner, 1987; Gunjan and Verreault, 2003; Libuda and Winston, 2006; Moran et al., 1990; Sutton et al., 2001; Vilardell and Warner, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Aneuploidy affects virtually all aspects of cell physiology, generally having a negative impact on fitness.
source: Given that aneuploidy has such a profound impact on the cell's transcriptome and proteome it is not surprising that aneuploidy affects virtually all aspects of cell physiology, generally having a negative impact on fitness (Hassold and Jacobs, 1984; Hodgkin, 2005; Huettel et al., 2008; Lindsley et al., 1972; Niwa et al., 2006; Stingele et al., 2012; Torres et al., 2007; Williams et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: When chromosome gains or losses lead to a decrease in growth rate, a stereotypic slow-growth transcriptional response known as the environmental stress response (ESR) ensues.
source: For example, when chromosome gains or losses lead to a decrease in growth rate, a stereotypic slow-growth transcriptional response known as the environmental stress response (ESR) ensues (Gasch et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The ESR is characterized by the down-regulation of growth-promoting genes and the up-regulation of stress response genes.
source: The ESR is characterized by the down-regulation of growth-promoting genes and the up-regulation of stress response genes and has been reported to occur in response to aneuploidy in many organisms including laboratory yeast strains (Sheltzer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim describes the characteristics of ESR and is supported by a citation.

claim: The ESR has been reported to occur in response to aneuploidy in many organisms including laboratory yeast strains.
source: The ESR is characterized by the down-regulation of growth-promoting genes and the up-regulation of stress response genes and has been reported to occur in response to aneuploidy in many organisms including laboratory yeast strains (Sheltzer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In mammals, an RNA-mediated mechanism silences expression of one copy of the X chromosome in females thereby equalizing X chromosome-encoded gene expression between males and females.
source: For example in mammals, an RNA-mediated mechanism silences expression of one copy of the X chromosome in females thereby equalizing X chromosome-encoded gene expression between males and females (Lee and Bartolomei, 2013).
evidence: This claim describes a well-known mechanism of dosage compensation in mammals and is supported by a citation.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, gene expression of the two X chromosomes is reduced by half in the hermaphrodite to match the expression of the single X chromosome in males.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, gene expression of the two X chromosomes is reduced by half in the hermaphrodite to match the expression of the single X chromosome in males (Meyer, 2010).
evidence: This claim describes dosage compensation in C. elegans and is supported by a citation.

claim: When an extra copy of the HTA1 gene (histone H2A) is introduced into budding yeast, mRNA turnover increases resulting in normal HTA1 transcript levels.
source: When an extra copy of the HTA1 gene (histone H2A) is introduced into budding yeast, mRNA turnover increases resulting in normal HTA1 transcript levels (Moran et al., 1990; Osley and Hereford, 1981).
evidence: This claim describes a specific example of dosage compensation in budding yeast and is supported by citations.

claim: Transcriptional responses to aneuploidy are elicited by an aneuploid genome affecting a biological pathway and are not restricted to the aneuploid chromosomes but impact expression of genes located throughout the genome.
source: Transcriptional responses to aneuploidy are elicited by an aneuploid genome affecting a biological pathway and are not restricted to the aneuploid chromosomes but impact expression of genes located throughout the genome.
evidence: This claim distinguishes transcriptional responses from dosage compensation based on established knowledge.

claim: Dosage compensation specifically alters the expression of a gene whose copy number has been varied and its effects are thus restricted to the aneuploid chromosome.
source: In contrast, dosage compensation specifically alters the expression of a gene whose copy number has been varied and its effects are thus restricted to the aneuploid chromosome.
evidence: This claim defines the characteristics of dosage compensation based on established knowledge.

claim: Experimental evolution studies suggest that selective pressures cause changes in karyotype such as chromosome gains or losses.
source: Experimental evolution studies suggest that selective pressures cause changes in karyotype such as chromosome gains or losses (Dunham et al., 2002; Gresham et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental evolution studies.

claim: Aneuploidies are usually transient evolutionary intermediates that, given time, are replaced with more optimal solutions.
source: However, such aneuploidies are usually transient evolutionary intermediates that, given time, are replaced with more optimal solutions (Yona et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) isolated 47 wild yeast strains to identify 12 (26%) that harbored whole chromosome gains and/or losses.
source: They isolated 47 wild yeast strains to identify 12 (26%) that harbored whole chromosome gains and/or losses.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings from the Hose et al. study.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) concluded that aneuploidies are prevalent, stable and well-tolerated in wild yeast strains.
source: The detailed analysis of six of these strains led them to the conclusion that aneuploidies are prevalent, stable and well-tolerated in wild yeast strains.
evidence: This is a statement about the conclusions drawn by Hose et al.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) concluded that tolerance to aneuploidy is caused by dosage compensation mechanisms that buffer gene amplifications thereby protecting cells against the adverse effects of aneuploidy.
source: Based on gene expression analyses, they further concluded that tolerance to aneuploidy is caused by dosage compensation mechanisms that buffer gene amplifications thereby protecting cells against the adverse effects of aneuploidy.
evidence: This is a statement about the conclusions drawn by Hose et al.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) reported that gene-dosage compensation functions at >30% of amplified genes.
source: They reported that gene-dosage compensation functions at >30% of amplified genes.
evidence: This is a specific quantitative claim from the Hose et al. study.

claim: Gene copy number and expression are tightly correlated in wild S. cerevisiae strains.
source: This reexamination revealed that gene copy number and expression are tightly correlated in wild S. cerevisiae strains.
evidence: This is a main finding of the current study based on reanalysis of the Hose et al. data.

claim: Dosage compensation is a rare occurrence in both laboratory and natural variants of S. cerevisiae.
source: We conclude that dosage compensation is a rare occurrence in both, laboratory and natural variants of S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the data analysis.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) determined karyotypes by inferring the copy number from genome sequencing data using depth of coverage.
source: Hose et al. (2015) isolated 47 wild yeast variants and determined their karyotypes by inferring the copy number from genome sequencing data using depth of coverage.
evidence: This describes the methodology used by Hose et al.

claim: 12 of 47 wild yeast strains isolated by Hose et al. (2015) harbor whole chromosome aneuploidies.
source: This analysis showed that 12 of these 47 strains harbor whole chromosome aneuploidies.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the Hose et al. study.

claim: DNA and RNA sequencing data for 6 of the 12 aneuploid strains were deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under accession SRP047341 and NCBI Gene Omnibus under accession GSE61532.
source: DNA and RNA sequencing data for 6 of these 12 aneuploid strains were deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under accession SRP047341 and NCBI Gene Omnibus under accession GSE61532 referenced in Hose et al. (2015).
evidence: This provides information about data availability from the Hose et al. study.

claim: Strain K9 is a diploid strain carrying an extra copy of chromosomes IX and X.
source: Strain K9 is a diploid strain carrying an extra copy of chromosomes IX and X (Figure 1A,G)
evidence: This is supported by the karyotype analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: YPS1009 is diploid with an extra copy of chromosome XII.
source: YPS1009 is diploid with an extra copy of chromosome XII (Figure 1B,G)
evidence: This is supported by the karyotype analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Diploid strain NCYC110 carries two extra copies of chromosome VIII.
source: and diploid strain NCYC110 carries two extra copies of chromosome VIII (Figure 1C,G).
evidence: This is supported by the karyotype analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Strains K9, YPS1009 and NCYC110 with low levels of aneuploidy harbor relatively stable karyotypes.
source: We examined the karyotypes and gene expression of these strains and found the aneuploid strains K9, YPS1009 and NCYC110 with low levels of aneuploidy to harbor relatively stable karyotypes (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is based on the analysis of karyotype data shown in Figure 1.

claim: RNA levels generally correlated well with DNA levels in strains K9, YPS1009 and NCYC110, with aneuploid chromosomes overall showing a corresponding increase in gene expression.
source: As discussed in more detail below, RNA levels also generally correlated well with DNA levels, with aneuploid chromosomes overall showing a corresponding increase in gene expression (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is based on the analysis of RNA and DNA data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Strain K9 which harbors extra copies of chromosome IX and X in the Hose et al. (2015) study was previously reported to be trisomic for chromosome IX only.
source: It is, however, noteworthy that strain K9 which harbors extra copies of chromosome IX and X in the Hose et al. (2015) study was previously reported to be trisomic for chromosome IX only, indicating that this strain exhibits some karyotypic instability (Kvitek et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on a comparison with a previous study, indicating karyotypic instability.

claim: Strains YJM428, Y2189, and K1 harbor complex karyotypes.
source: In contrast to the relatively stable strains K9, YPS1009, and NCYC110, a different picture emerged from our analysis of strains YJM428, Y2189, and K1 that harbor complex karyotypes.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of karyotype data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The described aneuploidies in strains YJM428, Y2189, and K1 are only present in subpopulations of cells.
source: Based on the presence of non-integer DNA copy number states, we conclude that the described aneuploidies are only present in subpopulations of cells (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is inferred from the non-integer DNA copy number states observed in the data.

claim: Some strains had changed their karyotypes between DNA and RNA analyses.
source: The comparison between RNA and DNA levels further revealed significant inconsistencies between the two data sets indicating that some strains had changed their karyotypes between the two analyses (e.g. DNA and RNA copy numbers are very different in strains Y2189 and K1; Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is inferred from inconsistencies between DNA and RNA data.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) used the standard deviations (SD) of the DNA measurements to establish cutoffs in their RNA data set to identify dosage compensated genes.
source: This discrepancy is problematic as Hose et al. (2015) used the standard deviations (SD) of the DNA measurements to establish cutoffs in their RNA data set to identify dosage compensated genes (discussed in detail below).
evidence: This describes a methodological issue with the Hose et al. analysis.

claim: Strain T73 is tetrasomic for chromosome VIII.
source: We found that strains T73, which is tetrasomic for chromosome VIII (analyzed below; Figure 4A)
evidence: This is based on karyotype analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Strain WE372 is trisomic for chromosome I.
source: and WE372, which is trisomic for chromosome I to harbor stable karyotypes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on karyotype analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: DNA copy numbers in strains UC5, Y3, Y6, and CBS7960 exhibited non-integer DNA copy number states indicating that the strains are heterogeneous.
source: However, DNA copy numbers in strains UC5, Y3, Y6, and CBS7960 exhibited non-integer DNA copy number states indicating that the strains are heterogeneous (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This is based on DNA copy number analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: More than half of the 35 wild strains analyzed by Hose et al. (2015) harbored karyotype profiles consistent with heterogeneity.
source: Analysis of the karyotypes of the other 35 wild strains (both Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1 in Hose et al. (2015)) revealed that more than half of the strains harbored karyotype profiles consistent with heterogeneity.
evidence: This is based on analysis of karyotype data from Hose et al.

claim: Strains K10, YJM308, and Y2209 utilized as the euploid reference in the gene expression analysis appeared to harbor heterogeneous karyotypes.
source: Importantly, strains K10, YJM308, and Y2209 utilized as the euploid reference in the gene expression analysis of the aneuploid wild strains YJM428, Y2189, K1, and K9 (Figure 2 in Hose et al., 2015) appeared to harbor heterogeneous karyotypes (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is based on karyotype analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Strain YJM308 harbors an amplification of chromosome XV and has lost part of chromosome III.
source: In particular, strain YJM308 harbors an amplification of chromosome XV and has lost part of chromosome III (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is based on karyotype analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Only 10.6% (5 out of 47) of the strains analyzed by Hose et al. (2015) harbor relatively stable aneuploidies that are confined to 1 – 2 chromosomes.
source: We conclude that only 10.6% (5 out of 47) of the strains analyzed by Hose et al. (2015) harbor relatively stable aneuploidies that are confined to 1 – 2 chromosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of karyotype data.

claim: All strains studied by Hose et al. (2015) were derived from single colonies.
source: As all strains studied by Hose et al. (2015) were derived from single colonies, our finding of significant karyotype heterogeneity indicates that a large fraction of wild yeast strains grown under standard laboratory conditions are unstable.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the Hose et al. study.

claim: A large fraction of wild yeast strains grown under standard laboratory conditions are unstable.
source: As all strains studied by Hose et al. (2015) were derived from single colonies, our finding of significant karyotype heterogeneity indicates that a large fraction of wild yeast strains grown under standard laboratory conditions are unstable.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed karyotype heterogeneity in strains derived from single colonies.

claim: The aneuploidies in wild isolates are likely a consequence of culturing the natural variants under laboratory conditions to which they may be ill-adapted, instead of these strains being naturally aneuploid.
source: The observed instability and heterogeneity of many wild S. cerevisiae strains makes it likely that the aneuploidies in these wild isolates are a consequence of culturing the natural variants under laboratory conditions to which they may be ill-adapted to, instead of these strains being naturally aneuploid.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed karyotype instability.

claim: Caution is warranted when analyzing growth rates, gene expression patterns and phenotypes of wild yeast strains under laboratory growth conditions.
source: Caution is therefore warranted when analyzing growth rates, gene expression patterns and phenotypes of such wild yeast strains under laboratory growth conditions.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the observed instability of wild yeast strains.

claim: RNA and DNA levels are well-correlated in haploid laboratory W303 strains carrying additional chromosomes.
source: In our previous studies, we found RNA and DNA levels to be well-correlated in haploid laboratory W303 strains carrying additional chromosomes (Dephoure et al., 2014; Torres et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings from the authors' own studies.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) reported that the coordination between DNA and RNA levels was not evident in wild budding yeast isolates.
source: Hose et al. (2015) reported that this coordination between DNA and RNA levels was not evident in wild budding yeast isolates.
evidence: This is a statement about the conclusions of the Hose et al. study.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) concluded that 38% (838 of 2,204) of amplified genes showed lower expression than predicted by their gene copy number.
source: Hose et al. (2015) compared mRNA levels with DNA copy number of amplified genes across six aneuploid wild yeast strains called K9, YPS1009, NCYC110, YJM428, Y2189, and K1 and concluded that 38% (838 of 2,204) of amplified genes showed lower expression than predicted by their gene copy number (light blue points in Figure 4A in Hose et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative claim from the Hose et al. study.

claim: The expression of all genes on the aneuploid chromosomes increased proportionally with gene copy number in strains YPS1009, K9, and NCYC110.
source: Our analysis revealed that the expression of all genes on the aneuploid chromosomes increased proportionally with gene copy number (Figure 1A–C, 3A,B).
evidence: This is based on the reanalysis of gene expression data shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: The log2 ratios of expression values of genes encoded by the triplicated chromosomes fit a normal distribution with a mean value very close to the predicted log2 ratio of 0.58.
source: As predicted by a null model with no compensation, we found that the log2 ratios of expression values of genes encoded by the triplicated chromosomes of these strains to fit a normal distribution with a mean value very close to the predicted log2 ratio of 0.58 (mean log2 ratio = 0.55, R2 = 0.99, Figure 3A, middle panel, Figure 3B) for the trisomic strains
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The log2 ratios of expression values of genes encoded by the tetrasomic chromosome fit a normal distribution with a mean log2 ratio of 0.95.
source: and a log2 ratio of 1 (mean log2 ratio = 0.95, R2 = 0.97, Figure 3A, right panel) for the tetrasomic chromosome.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 3.

claim: No skewness in the distributions was noted for trisomic and tetrasomic chromosomes.
source: No skewness in the distributions - more compensating or exacerbating - was noted as would be expected if a large fraction of the genes encoded on the aneuploid chromosome were dosage compensated (skewness = 0.02 (3n) and 0.07 (4n); Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The distribution of log2 ratios of expression values of genes encoded by euploid chromosomes fit a normal distribution with the predicted log2 ratio of 0.
source: The distribution of log2 ratios of expression values of genes encoded by euploid chromosomes also fit a normal distribution with the predicted log2 ratio of 0 (mean log2 ratio = 0.00, R2 = 0.99, Figure 3A left panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The log2 ratios of expression values of genes encoded by duplicated chromosomes in disomic W303 strains fit a normal distribution with a mean value very close to the predicted log2 ratio of 1.
source: RNA quantification of two disomic W303 strains (disomes V and XVI) showed that the log2 ratios of expression values of genes encoded by the duplicated chromosomes fit a normal distribution with a mean value very close to the predicted log2 ratio of 1 (mean log2 ratio = 1.03, R2 = 0.98, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene expression data from laboratory strains shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Between 0% (0 gene in NCYC110) and 3% (19 genes in K9) of amplified genes showed values lower than expected using 2 SD from the means as cutoff.
source: To determine how many genes were potentially subject to dosage compensation, we used 2 SD from the means of the log2 ratios of each amplified chromosome and found that between 0% (0 gene in NCYC110) and 3% (19 genes in K9) of amplified genes showed values lower than expected (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gene expression data shown in Table 1.

claim: A similar number of genes exhibited higher than expected expression (between 1% in YPS1009 and 2% in NCYC110).
source: Importantly, a similar number of genes was found to exhibit higher than expected expression (between 1% in YPS1009 and 2% in NCYC110, Table 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gene expression data shown in Table 1.

claim: Using the same cutoff on the euploid chromosomes, between 0.1% (7 genes in NCYC110) and 3% (153 genes in K1) genes showed values lower than expected.
source: Using the same cutoff on the euploid chromosomes, we found between 0.1% (7 genes in NCYC110) and 3% (153 genes in K1) genes with values lower than expected.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gene expression data.

claim: The nature of the distributions of gene expression patterns (normal distribution with expected means) is inconsistent with high levels of dosage compensation occurring in wild yeast strains.
source: The nature of the distributions of gene expression patterns (normal distribution with expected means) and these analyses are inconsistent with high levels of dosage compensation occurring in wild yeast strains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis of gene expression data.

claim: Gene expression proportionally increases with copy number without signs of dosage compensation in wild yeast strains.
source: Instead, they indicate that gene expression proportionally increases with copy number without signs of dosage compensation in wild yeast strains.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the statistical analysis of gene expression data.

claim: Any effects on gene expression seen in these strains are likely to be the consequence of measurement noise or a transcriptional response elicited by the aneuploid state rather than dosage compensation.
source: The fact that the euploid chromosomes encode the same proportion of up and downregulated genes as the aneuploid chromosomes further indicates that any effects on gene expression seen in these strains are likely to be the consequence of measurement noise or a transcriptional response elicited by the aneuploid state rather than dosage compensation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of gene expression patterns between euploid and aneuploid chromosomes.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) generated a panel of isogenic euploid and aneuploid strain pairs.
source: To further characterize dosage compensation in wild variants Hose et al. (2015) generated a panel of isogenic euploid and aneuploid strain pairs.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used by Hose et al.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) isolated a disomic strain for chromosome VIII (YPS163-chr VIII-2n) of the euploid strain YPS163.
source: They isolated a disomic strain for chromosome VIII (YPS163-chr VIII-2n) of the euploid strain YPS163
evidence: This describes the strains generated by Hose et al.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) isolated euploid versions of strain T73, which is tetrasomic for chromosome VIII (T73-chrVIII-4n).
source: and euploid versions of strain T73, which is tetrasomic for chromosome VIII (T73-chrVIII-4n)
evidence: This describes the strains generated by Hose et al.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) isolated euploid versions of strain YJM428, which is tetrasomic for chromosome XVI (YJM428-chrXVI-4n).
source: and of strain YJM428, which is tetrasomic for chromosome XVI (YJM428-chrXVI-4n).
evidence: This describes the strains generated by Hose et al.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) concluded that between 11 and 36% of genes were expressed at lower than expected levels in the isogenic strain pairs.
source: They then determined DNA copy number state and gene expression levels in these strains and concluded that between 11 and 36% of genes were expressed at lower than expected levels, that is, they were dosage compensated.
evidence: This is a statement about the conclusions of the Hose et al. study.

claim: RNA levels proportionally increased with DNA copy number in aneuploid strains YPS163, T73, and YJM428.
source: We compared the average chromosome copy number in the three aneuploid strains with the average RNA copy number in these strains and found that RNA levels proportionally increased with DNA copy number (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is based on the reanalysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The 941 duplicated genes in strains YPS163, T73, and YJM428 showed a mean log2 ratio of 1.02 for DNA copy number and a nearly identical mean log2 ratio of 0.97 for RNA copy number.
source: The 941 duplicated genes showed a mean log2 ratio of 1.02 (SD = 0.29, R2 = 0.99) for DNA copy number and a nearly identical mean log2 ratio (mean = 0.97; SD = 0.36, R2 = 0.99) for RNA copy number (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The distribution of expression values in strains YPS163, T73, and YJM428 fit a normal distribution and was indistinguishable from the distribution of the gene expression values of genes encoded by the euploid chromosomes.
source: Furthermore, the distribution of expression values fit a normal distribution and was indistinguishable from the distribution of the gene expression values of genes encoded by the euploid chromosomes.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gene expression data.

claim: The standard deviations of the RNA distributions were similar for euploid and aneuploid chromosomes in strains YPS163, T73, and YJM428.
source: The standard deviations of the RNA distributions were similar for euploid and aneuploid chromosomes (Figure 4C bottom graphs) and each distribution showed skewness of 0.01 and 0.02, respectively.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: If dosage compensation were to occur, variance and skewness would be different between genes encoded by euploid and aneuploid chromosomes.
source: If dosage compensation were to occur, variance and skewness, would be different between genes encoded by euploid and aneuploid chromosomes.
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on statistical reasoning.

claim: Using 2 SD as cutoff to find potential dosage compensated genes, a small number of outliers was identified with similar numbers of up and downregulated outliers.
source: Lastly, using 2 SD as cutoff to find potential dosage compensated genes, we identified a small number of outliers. Importantly, the number of up and downregulated outliers was similar (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 5.

claim: RNA levels correlate well with DNA copy number in aneuploid strains YPS163, T73, and YJM428.
source: We conclude that RNA levels correlate well with DNA copy number in aneuploid strains YPS163, T73, and YJM428.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the reanalysis of gene expression data.

claim: Starting with strain YPS1009, which carries three copies of chromosome XII (YPS1090-chrXII-3n), Hose et al. (2015) derived a euploid strain (YPS1009-chrXII-2n) and a strain that is tetrasomic for chromosome XII (YPS1009-chr XII-4n).
source: Starting with strain YPS1009, which carries three copies of chromosome XII (YPS1090-chrXII-3n), Hose et al. (2015) derived a euploid strain (YPS1009-chrXII-2n) and a strain that is tetrasomic for chromosome XII (YPS1009-chr XII-4n; Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This describes the strains generated by Hose et al.

claim: Using strain NCYC110, which carries four copies of chromosome VIII (NCYC110-chrVIII-4n), Hose et al. (2015) isolated a strain trisomic for chromosome VIII (NCYC110-chrVIII-3n) and a diploid strain (NCYC110-chrVIII-2n).
source: Using strain NCYC110, which carries four copies of chromosome VIII (NCYC110-chrVIII-4n), they isolated a strain trisomic for chromosome VIII (NCYC110-chrVIII-3n) and a diploid strain (NCYC110-chrVIII-2n; Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This describes the strains generated by Hose et al.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) concluded that 11% of genes encoded on chromosome VIII and 29% of genes encoded on chromosome XII were dosage compensated.
source: They then determined DNA copy number state and gene expression levels in these strain series and concluded that 11% of genes encoded on chromosome VIII and 29% of genes encoded on chromosome XII were dosage compensated.
evidence: This is a statement about the conclusions of the Hose et al. study.

claim: The gene expression distribution of genes located on euploid and aneuploid chromosomes in the YPS1009 and NCYC110 strain series fit normal distributions without any skewness.
source: We found the gene expression distribution of genes located on euploid and aneuploid chromosomes to fit normal distributions without any skewness (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The two trisomic strains YPS1009-chrXII-3n and NCYC110-chrVIII-3n together harbored 776 triplicated genes with an averaged log2 ratio of DNA copy number of 0.57 and 0.60 for RNA copy number.
source: The two trisomic strains YPS1009-chrXII-3n and NCYC110-chrVIII-3n together harbored 776 triplicated genes. Their averaged log2 ratio of DNA copy number was 0.57 (SD = 0.15, R2 = 0.99) and 0.60 (SD = 0.53, R2 = 0.97) for RNA copy number (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In the tetrasomic strains, the mean log2 ratio of DNA copy number of genes located on the tetrasomic chromosome was 0.99 and the mean mRNA expression was 0.99.
source: A similar coordination between DNA and RNA copy number was observed in the tetrasomic strains. The mean log2 ratio of DNA copy number of genes located on the tetrasomic chromosome was 0.99 (SD = 0.16, R2 = 0.99), the mean mRNA expression of genes located on the tetrasomic chromosome was 0.99 (SD = 0.62, R2 = 0.96; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The distributions of DNA and mRNA copy number were similar for genes located on euploid, trisomic and tetrasomic chromosomes, with similar SDs and no evidence of skewness.
source: Importantly, the distributions of DNA and mRNA copy number were similar for genes located on euploid, trisomic and tetrasomic chromosomes, with similar SDs and no evidence of skewness (skewness varied between 0.00 and 0.03).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gene expression data.

claim: Dosage compensation was not detected in the strains described in Hose et al. (2015).
source: In summary, we were not been able to detect dosage compensation in the strains described in Hose et al. (2015).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the reanalysis of all the gene expression data.

claim: RNA levels of genes encoded by the aneuploid chromosomes are normally distributed with the expected or close to expected mean.
source: RNA levels of genes encoded by the aneuploid chromosomes are normally distributed with the expected or close to expected mean.
evidence: This is a summary of the statistical analysis of gene expression data.

claim: No difference was observed between the number of down-regulated genes located on aneuploid and euploid chromosomes.
source: No difference was observed between the number of down-regulated genes located on aneuploid and euploid chromosomes.
evidence: This is based on the statistical analysis of gene expression data.

claim: No skewness was observed for any of the distributions of gene expression in the analyzed strains.
source: Furthermore, no skewness was observed for any of the distributions.
evidence: This is based on the statistical analysis of gene expression data.

claim: Distributions exhibit negative values of skewness when dosage compensation occurs.
source: Figure 7 shows how distributions exhibit negative values of skewness when dosage compensation occurs.
evidence: This is a theoretical demonstration shown in Figure 7.

claim: In a previous study, attenuation in the expression of certain genes in aneuploid yeast strains was detected using the method employed in this study.
source: Importantly, in a previous study, we were able to detect attenuation in the expression of certain genes in aneuploid yeast strains using the method employed here.
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors demonstrating the sensitivity of their method.

claim: Production of ribosomal proteins encoded on disomic chromosomes is significantly attenuated causing the distributions to exhibit negative skewness.
source: In Dephoure et al. (2014), we examined the proteomes of haploid disomic laboratory yeast strains and found that production of ribosomal proteins encoded on disomic chromosomes is significantly attenuated causing the distributions to exhibit negative skewness (Dephoure et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a specific finding from a previous study by the authors.

claim: The ratios in the Hose et al. data are off by a factor of log2 = 0.1–0.2 due to normalization issues.
source: The first regards data normalization. The ratios are off by a factor of log2 = 0.1–0.2 (normalized data utilized in Hose et al. (2015) were kindly provided by A. Gasch).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the normalized data provided by Hose et al.

claim: Most normalization protocols do not take into account that aneuploid strains harbor a different number of gene copies compared to euploid strains.
source: Most normalization protocols do not take into account that aneuploid strains harbor a different number of gene copies compared to euploid strains.
evidence: This is a statement about common practices in data normalization.

claim: When normalization does not account for different gene copy numbers, data are shifted by a factor that depends on the degree of aneuploidy and results in incorrect values.
source: When this is not manually corrected, data are shifted by a factor that depends on the degree of aneuploidy and results in incorrect values as shown in Figure 8A.
evidence: This is an explanation of the normalization problem, illustrated in Figure 8A.

claim: The degree by which the data used for analysis by Hose et al. (2015) deviate from the correctly normalized expression values is of the same magnitude as some of the cutoffs used to define dosage compensated genes.
source: The degree by which the data used for analysis by Hose et al. (2015) deviate from the correctly normalized expression values is of the same magnitude as some of the cutoffs used to define dosage compensated genes (detailed next).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of normalization errors and cutoff values.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) used the SD of the DNA measurements, which ranged between 0.1 and 0.45, as cutoffs for the RNA measurements.
source: To establish cutoffs for designating whether a gene is dosage compensated or not Hose et al. (2015) used the SD of the DNA measurements, which ranged between 0.1 and 0.45 (Table 1 column 11, data kindly provided by A. Gasch) as cutoffs for the RNA measurements (Figure 4 in Hose et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the methodology used by Hose et al., with data shown in Table 1.

claim: Genes whose expression deviated by the DNA SD value from the expected RNA expression level were considered dosage compensated by Hose et al. (2015).
source: Genes whose expression deviated by the DNA SD value from the expected RNA expression level were considered dosage compensated.
evidence: This describes the criteria used by Hose et al. to identify dosage compensated genes.

claim: The DNA copy number measurements are less variable than mRNA measurements.
source: This is not the correct cutoff tool because the DNA copy number measurements are less variable than mRNA measurements.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of the measurements, supported by the data.

claim: Transcript levels can vary by several orders of magnitude depending on the expression levels of a particular gene.
source: As seen in Figure 8B, transcript levels can vary by several orders of magnitude depending on the expression levels of a particular gene.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 8B.

claim: The distributions of relative RNA changes will show bigger SDs than gene copy number distributions.
source: Therefore, the distributions of relative RNA changes will show bigger SDs than gene copy number distributions.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the variability of transcript levels.

claim: The RNA measurements conducted by Hose et al. (2015) show SDs between 0.53 and 1.01.
source: Indeed, the RNA measurements conducted by Hose et al. (2015) show SDs between 0.53 and 1.01 (Table 1, column 6).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Table 1.

claim: Employing the SD derived from the DNA measurements will not identify genes that are dosage compensated in a statistically significant manner.
source: Employing the SD derived from the DNA measurements, which are fairly lower (Table 1, column 8), will therefore not identify genes that are dosage compensated in a statistically significant manner (see false discovery rate discussion below).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of DNA and RNA measurement variability.

claim: Genes identified in Figure 4 of Hose et al. (2015) as dosage compensated were included in a group of 245 dosage compensated genes used to establish GO term enrichments among dosage compensated genes.
source: This is of particular importance as genes identified in Figure 4 of Hose et al. (2015) as dosage compensated were included in a group of 245 dosage compensated genes used to establish GO term enrichments among dosage compensated genes.
evidence: This describes how the genes identified by Hose et al. were used in further analysis.

claim: The null model shown by the diagonal of equal RNA and DNA in Figure 4A of Hose et al. (2015) did not bisect the blue (compensated) and magenta (exacerbated) points.
source: Figure 4A in Hose et al. (2015) displays an unusual behavior. The null model shown by the diagonal of equal RNA and DNA in this figure did not bisect the blue (compensated) and magenta (exacerbated) points.
evidence: This is an observation about the presentation of data in the Hose et al. paper.

claim: The vast majority of points below the null model line in Figure 4A of Hose et al. (2015) were considered compensated while the vast majority of points above this line were considered not exacerbated.
source: Instead, the vast majority of points below this line were considered compensated while the vast majority of points above this line were considered not exacerbated.
evidence: This is an observation about how genes were classified in the Hose et al. analysis.

claim: There could be a high number of false positives amongst the 838 genes determined to be dosage compensated by Hose et al. (2015).
source: This suggests that there could be a high number of false positives amongst the 838 genes determined to be dosage compensated.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of the data presentation.

claim: Based on 10,000 randomizations, on average 779 genes would have passed the threshold method used by Hose et al. (2015) by chance.
source: Based on 10,000 randomizations, we determined that on average, 779 genes would have passed the threshold method used by Hose et al. (2015) by chance.
evidence: This is based on a permutation analysis to determine false discovery rate.

claim: The false discovery rate for the Hose et al. (2015) analysis is 92.9%.
source: This yields a false discovery rate (FDR) of 92.9%.
evidence: This is calculated from the permutation analysis.

claim: The FDR was between 93 and 100% at cutoffs from 0.1 STD to 2 STDs.
source: This high false discovery rate was also seen at much lower cutoffs. The FDR was between 93 and 100% at cutoffs from 0.1 STD to 2 STDs.
evidence: This is based on the permutation analysis at different cutoff values.

claim: Using a second method based on measurement noise distribution, on average 754 genes would have passed the effective threshold used by Hose et al. (2015).
source: Using this method, we found that on average, 754 genes would have passed the effective threshold used by Hose et al. (2015).
evidence: This is based on a second method to calculate false discovery rate.

claim: The second method for calculating FDR corresponds to a false discovery rate of 89%.
source: This corresponds to a false discovery rate of 89%; this value is likely a small underestimation of FDR given our method for estimation of DNA error.
evidence: This is calculated from the second method of FDR analysis.

claim: Both methods applied to determine false discovery rate strongly suggest that only a handful, at most ~70 genes or <3%, are actually dosage compensated.
source: We conclude that both methods that we applied to determine false discovery rate strongly suggest that only a handful, at most ~70 genes or <3%, are actually dosage compensated.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the two FDR analyses.

claim: The FDR results are completely in line with previous findings from laboratory strains.
source: These results are completely in line with previous findings from laboratory strains (Springer et al., 2010; Dephoure et al., 2014; Torres et al., 2007).
evidence: This connects the current findings to previous studies.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) defined genes to be dosage compensated when the RNA levels did not increase with DNA copy number in their YPS1009 and NCYC110 ploidy series.
source: In a second approach to identify dosage compensated genes, Hose et al. (2015) defined genes to be dosage compensated when the RNA levels did not increase with DNA copy number in their YPS1009 (2N, 2N+1 chromosome XII, 2N+2 chromosomes XII) and NCYC110 (2N, 2N+1 chromosome VIII, 2N+2 chromosomes VIII) ploidy series.
evidence: This describes the second method used by Hose et al. to identify dosage compensated genes.

claim: Hose et al. (2015) developed a mixture of linear regression (MLR) model to classify genes based on the slope and intercept of the RNA-gene copy relationships.
source: For this, they developed a mixture of linear regression (MLR) model to classify genes based on the slope and intercept of the RNA-gene copy relationships.
evidence: This describes the methodology used by Hose et al.

claim: When RNA levels did not increase proportionately as DNA copy increased as evidenced by slopes lower than 1 in the MLR model, a gene was classified as dosage compensated and categorized as Class 3a by Hose et al. (2015).
source: When RNA levels did not increase proportionately as DNA copy increased as evidenced by slopes lower than 1 in the MLR model, a gene was classified as dosage compensated and categorizes as Class 3a in Table 1 in Hose et al. (2015).
evidence: This describes the classification criteria used by Hose et al.

claim: Thirty genes on chromosome VIII and 142 genes on chromosome XII were identified as dosage compensated through the MLR method by Hose et al. (2015).
source: Thirty genes on chromosome VIII and 142 genes on chromosome XII were identified as dosage compensated through this method.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the Hose et al. study.

claim: The MLR method of identifying dosage compensated genes is problematic because there are only three data points per analysis.
source: This method of identifying dosage compensated genes is problematic in several ways. First, because there are only three data points per analysis, a single deviating data point can have a significant impact on the slope.
evidence: This is a critique of the methodology based on statistical reasoning.

claim: A gene with values of log2 ratio = 0.3, 0.6 and 0.8 representing two, three, and four copies will perfectly fit a straight line with the slope of 0.5 and would be classified as dosage compensated according to the criteria in Hose et al. (2015) even though none of the three data points significantly deviates from the mean value given a SD of 0.3 or higher.
source: For example, a gene with values of log2 ratio = 0.3, 0.6 and 0.8 representing, two, three, and four copies, respectively, will perfectly fit a straight line with the slope of 0.5 and hence would be classified as dosage compensated according to the criteria in Hose et al. (2015) even though none of the three data points significantly deviates from the mean value given a SD of 0.3 or higher (Figure 8C, Table 2).
evidence: This is an example demonstrating the problem with the MLR method, illustrated in Figure 8C and Table 2.

claim: The majority (103 of 172) of class 3a genes fit the MLR model with slopes of 0.5 or higher indicating that their gene expression increases with copy number.
source: In fact, the majority (103 of 172) of class 3a genes (Table 1 and Supplemental File 3 in Hose et al. (2015)) fit the MLR model with slopes of 0.5 or higher indicating that their gene expression increases with copy number.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the genes classified as dosage compensated by Hose et al.

claim: Only two genes on aneuploid chromosome VIII and seven genes on aneuploid chromosome XII show log2 ratios 1 SD lower than the mean in three biological replicates and were reproducibly lower when present in 3 or 4 copies.
source: In the first, we calculated the mean and standard deviations for each of the biological replicates in the NCYC110 and YPS1009 strain series and found that only two genes on aneuploid chromosome VIII and seven genes on aneuploid chromosome XII show log2 ratios 1 SD lower than the mean in three biological replicates and were reproducibly lower when present in 3 or 4 copies.
evidence: This is based on reanalysis of the gene expression data from the strain series.

claim: Not a single gene passed the cutoff of 2 SD below the mean in the NCYC110 and YPS1009 strain series.
source: Not a single gene passed the cutoff of 2 SD below the mean.
evidence: This is based on reanalysis of the gene expression data from the strain series.

claim: For the majority of genes identified as dosage compensated by the MLR method, only one of the two data points supports the conclusion that a gene is expressed at lower than the expected value.
source: We conclude that for the majority of genes only one of the two data points supports the conclusion that a gene is expressed at lower than the expected value, calling into question that the genes identified by this approach are indeed dosage compensated.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the reanalysis of the gene expression data.

claim: The false discovery rate for the MLR method used by Hose et al. (2015) was within error of 100%.
source: From this analysis we determined the false discovery rate was within error of 100%.
evidence: This is based on a permutation analysis to determine FDR for the MLR method.

claim: There is no significant dosage compensation in the YPS1009 and NCYC110 aneuploid series.
source: We conclude that there is no significant dosage compensation in these aneuploid series.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the FDR analysis.

claim: A large fraction of wild S. cerevisiae strains are unstable and heterogeneous when grown under laboratory conditions.
source: Our analyses indicate that a large fraction of wild S. cerevisiae strains are unstable and heterogeneous when grown under laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the karyotype analysis.

claim: At least some wild S. cerevisiae strains may not be naturally aneuploid but could become aneuploid due to an adaptive response to laboratory growth conditions.
source: This result suggests that at least some wild S. cerevisiae strains may not be naturally aneuploid but could become aneuploid due to an adaptive response to laboratory growth conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed karyotype instability.

claim: Reevaluation of the DNA and RNA copy number data generated by Hose et al. (2015) indicates that dosage compensation is rare in both wild and laboratory strain of S. cerevisiae.
source: Reevaluation of the DNA and RNA copy number data generated by Hose et al. (2015) further indicates that dosage compensation is rare in both wild and laboratory strain of S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the reanalysis of gene expression data.

claim: Both wild and laboratory strains of S. cerevisiae lack mechanisms that allow them to attenuate gene expression in response to gene copy number alterations.
source: Both types of strains lack mechanisms that allow them to attenuate gene expression in response to gene copy number alterations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the finding that dosage compensation is rare in both types of strains.

claim: Wild variants of S. cerevisiae do not have mechanisms in place that protect them from changes in gene copy number.
source: We conclude that wild variants of S. cerevisiae do not have mechanisms in place that protect them from changes in gene copy number.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The regulation of gene expression in wild variants of S. cerevisiae is the same as that of laboratory strains of budding yeast.
source: Their regulation of gene expression is thus the same as that of laboratory strains of budding yeast.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the comparison of gene expression patterns.
